growth_story.headline: A gas boom lifted Trinidad and Tobago fast; since energy prices and output fell in 2015, income per person has slid back to its 2006 level.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Trinidad and Tobago grew 3.9 percent a year in 1990–1997, climbing back from a long slide through the 1980s. Then came a gas boom: growth averaged 8.6 percent a year in 1998–2006, as heavy spending on new natural gas plants and good prices lifted energy output fast. Growth slowed to 2.1 percent a year in 2007–2014, and income per person reached its peak in 2014. From 2015 world energy prices fell and gas and oil output dropped, and growth has averaged -1.8 percent a year in 2015–2025, with deep falls in 2016 and in the pandemic year of 2020. In 2025 income per person was still 19.2 percent below its 2014 peak, about where it first was in 2006, and the sources describe an aging energy sector that weighs on growth while manufacturing and services carry what growth there is.

threads.title: The natural gas boom
threads.text: In the early 2000s the energy sector grew very fast, driven by good prices and large new natural gas plants. The IMF then described the country as having the strongest growth in its region. This is the boom behind the 1998–2006 era.

threads.title: The 2015 energy price shock
threads.text: In 2015 world energy prices fell sharply just as maintenance work and falling gas and oil production cut energy output. Budget deficits surged and the economy shrank, opening the era of decline that began in 2015.

since_last_year.text: The recovery stalled again. In mid-2026 the IMF expected modest growth for 2025, but the World Bank's October 2026 estimate is that the economy shrank, because gains in energy could not make up for weaker activity elsewhere. The World Bank projects a small contraction in 2026 too. The war in the Middle East has pushed up energy prices, which the IMF expects to lift energy export revenue for now.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a gradual recovery that continued in 2025. The data show a deeper and older fall: income per person dropped 0.7 percent in 2025 and is still 19.2 percent below its 2014 peak, a decline that began well before the pandemic. The two institutions also disagree on 2025 itself. The IMF reports growth, while the World Bank estimates that the economy shrank.
